teaser: No head, no arms, no feet. And still she looks like she is about to take off.
review_notes:
Date: pilot.json gives -190. The usual label is 'about 190 BC', but scholars propose dates between roughly 220 and 185 BC, and the naval victory it celebrates is not identified. Lesson says 'around 190 BC' and 'nobody knows which battle'.
Discovery by Charles Champoiseau, French vice-consul, on Samothrace in April 1863; ship blocks understood in 1875 (Austrian archaeologists) and brought to Paris in 1879.
Heights: statue about 2.75 m, whole monument about 5.57 m (Louvre figures).
Marbles: white Parian marble for the figure, gray marble from Rhodes (Lartos) for the ship.
Right wing: a plaster reconstruction made in the 19th century as a mirror image of the left one. The lesson says the wing seen in this photo is the ancient left wing, because the photo shows the statue's left side with the prow pointing to the viewer's left. Please confirm.
Right hand found in 1950, shown in a case near the statue; open palm, so she probably held no trumpet.
The claim that the statue was designed to be seen in three-quarter view from its left (the other side being less finished).
Evacuation from the Louvre in September 1939 down a wooden ramp on the staircase, to the Château de Valençay.
Nike swoosh: designed in 1971 by student Carolyn Davidson for 35 dollars, commonly described as evoking the goddess's wing (the goddess in general, not this statue specifically).
Navel visible through the cloth at about (0.48, 0.275): visible in our image, check on the zoom file.

lesson.text: Start with the inventory of what is gone. The head. Both arms. Both feet. One whole wing, which the museum had to rebuild in plaster. Whatever she held, whatever her face expressed, the paint that once colored her. By any normal count, this is a wreck.

And yet she is one of the three or four most visited objects in the Louvre. People climb a long staircase toward her and stop talking. So the useful question is not what is missing. It is what is left that can do this to a crowd.

She is Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, always shown with wings because victory arrives fast and can fly off again. She was carved around 190 BC, in a period called Hellenistic, when Greek sculptors loved drama, motion and strong feeling. Under her feet is the gray stone front of a warship. She has just landed on its deck.
The whole monument is built from three directions that pull against each other.

lines.label: The ship
lines.text: The prow, the pointed front of the ship, drives toward the left. That is the direction of travel, straight into the wind.

lines.label: The body
lines.text: She leans forward from the ankles, chest ahead of her hips, like someone bracing on a moving deck. Her weight has not settled yet.

lines.label: The wing
lines.text: The wing sweeps up and back, still open to slow her down. Body forward, wing back: this tug in two directions is what reads as movement.

lesson.text: The sculptor did not carve a goddess standing on a boat. He carved one instant: the touch-down, when the wings are still working and the cloth has not yet fallen still.

She was found in April 1863 on Samothrace, a small Greek island, by Charles Champoiseau, a French diplomat digging in an ancient sanctuary. She came out of the ground in many pieces. The big gray blocks nearby were left behind: nobody understood they were a ship until twelve years later.

Now the wind, since you cannot carve air. The sculptor makes it visible through what it does to cloth. Her dress is a thin tunic, belted under the chest, with a heavier cloak that has slipped down around her hips. The stone is marble from the island of Paros, prized because it can be cut very fine.

lesson.title: Carving the wind
lesson.text: Three places where stone behaves like wet fabric in a gale.

spots.title: Cloth like water
spots.text: Over the stomach the tunic is pressed so flat by the wind that the navel shows through it. The marble here is carved into a skin of thin ripples.

spots.title: Deep folds
spots.text: Lower down, the cloak twists between her legs in thick ropes with dark hollows cut far into the block. Thin cloth above, heavy cloth below: the contrast makes both convincing.

spots.title: A sail of stone
spots.text: Behind her hip, a fold of the cloak balloons backward, caught by the air. It is solid marble, hanging in space.

lesson.text: This trick has a name: wet drapery, cloth carved as if soaked so that it clings to the body and reveals it. Greek sculptors had used it for two centuries. Here it is pushed to an extreme, and it gives the figure a second job. You read her body and the weather at the same time.

In ancient Samothrace she stood outdoors, high on a hillside above the sanctuary, probably set up to thank the gods for a win at sea. Nobody knows which battle. She was meant to be seen at an angle from her left side, close to the angle of this photograph, and the sculptor finished the other side with less care.

In 1950, almost ninety years after the statue, archaeologists on Samothrace dug up her right hand. The palm is open and the fingers hold nothing. That ended an old theory that she was blowing a trumpet: she was most likely just raising her arm in greeting. The hand now sits in a glass case near her.

The Louvre placed her at the top of its grand staircase in the 1880s, on her rebuilt ship. The whole monument stands about 5.5 meters high (18 feet), the figure alone about 2.75 meters (9 feet). The choice of spot was a piece of theater: you approach her from below, as if from the water.

In September 1939, with war beginning, the Louvre emptied its galleries. The Victory, weighing several tons, was eased down the staircase on a wooden ramp, held by ropes, while the curators watched in silence. She spent the war hidden in a castle in the French countryside and came back unharmed.

One last thought about the missing parts. With a face, she would be a particular woman with a particular expression, and you would look there first. Without one, your eye has nowhere to rest except the motion itself. The damage turned a statue of a goddess into something closer to a statue of flight.

Her name went on to an unexpected career. In 1971 a young American shoe company called itself Nike, after the goddess, and paid a design student 35 dollars for a logo meant to suggest a wing in motion.

Before you leave her, go over the surface on your own. Several of the things listed as missing at the start have left traces you can find: a neck, a shoulder, the spot where a foot once pressed on the deck.

spots.title: The neck
spots.text: A stump of neck is all that remains above the shoulders. Its tilt suggests the head was turned slightly, toward the direction the ship is heading.

spots.title: Feathers
spots.text: This is the ancient wing. Short, scale-like feathers near the top give way to long flight feathers, each carved on its own, the way a real bird's wing is layered.

spots.title: The lost arm
spots.text: The shoulder ends in a break. The arm on this side is gone, and the tunic gathers in fine folds around the gap.

spots.title: Touching down
spots.text: The hem swirls around the place where her feet met the deck. Both feet are lost, yet the pose still shows one leg forward and one trailing.

spots.title: The prow
spots.text: The front of the warship, in gray marble from Rhodes, darker and rougher than the white figure. The change of stone separates the goddess from the world of men.

spots.title: The deck
spots.text: Long stepped ledges run along the side of the ship. They copy the wooden boxes that held the oars on a real Greek war galley.

quiz.question: What is the statue standing on?
quiz.explanation: The gray base is the prow of a ship, on whose deck she has just landed.

quiz.question: What is “wet drapery”?
options: Cloth carved as if soaked, so it clings to the body
A statue made for a fountain
quiz.explanation: The thin tunic is carved clinging to her, which reveals the body and shows the wind.

quiz.question: What did the hand found in 1950 reveal?
options: Her palm was open and held nothing
quiz.explanation: The empty open hand suggests a simple gesture of greeting.

quiz.question: Why is Nike shown with wings?
options: Victory arrives fast and can fly away again
She was the goddess of birds
Wings were a sign of royalty
quiz.explanation: The wings express how quickly victory comes and goes.

quiz.question: Where was the statue discovered?
options: In the cellars of the Louvre
quiz.explanation: A French diplomat dug her up there in 1863, in many pieces.

quiz.question: Which part of the statue did the museum rebuild in plaster?
quiz.explanation: One whole wing was missing and was reconstructed.

facts.text: The head of the Winged Victory is kept in a glass case near the statue.
facts.explanation: The head was never found. It is her right hand that sits in a case nearby.

facts.text: The figure and the ship are carved from two different kinds of marble.
facts.explanation: The goddess is white marble from Paros, the ship gray marble from Rhodes.

facts.text: During World War II the statue stayed at the top of its staircase.
facts.explanation: In 1939 it was lowered down a wooden ramp and hidden in a castle.
